hints: 1a (Brute Force). Since n <= 5, there are at most 105 non-negative integers with at most n digits.
1b (Brute Force). Check every integer from 0 to 10n - 1, and keep the largest one whose digit sum is s.
2a (Greedy). If s > 9 * n, no valid integer exists.
2b (Greedy). To maximize the integer, assign as much of the remaining digit sum as possible to each digit from left to right.
problems.name: Largest Integer With Given Digit Sum

hints: Merge the timestamps from both series in increasing order, similarly to the merge step of merge sort.
Because a missing timestamp uses the next available value, process the merged timestamps from right to left while maintaining the next available value in each series.
At each timestamp, update the maintained value for every series containing that timestamp, then add the two maintained values to the answer.
problems.name: Aggregate Two Time Series

hints: Count all sequences of k positive integers with sum n, then subtract those whose product is odd.
Using stars and bars, the total number of such sequences is C(n - 1, k - 1).
The product is odd exactly when every element is odd. Write each element as 2 * x + 1 and count the resulting non-negative solutions.
If n - k is odd, no sequence consisting entirely of odd integers exists. Otherwise, subtract C((n + k) / 2 - 1, k - 1).
problems.name: Count Valid Sequences

hints: Treat each state as (i, j, parity), where parity indicates whether the next action is odd-numbered or even-numbered.
From each state, consider moving to every adjacent cell and also waiting. Every transition changes the parity.
The transition cost depends on whether the chosen move follows the current parity rule. Waiting costs penalty[i][j].
All transition costs are non-negative, so use Dijkstra's algorithm on these states. The answer is the minimum distance to the destination with either parity.
problems.name: Minimum Cost Path with Alternating Directions III
